title: How HVAC distributors handle equipment matchups and AHRI data online
summary: HVAC distributors list AHRI-certified matchups as records linking outdoor unit, coil or air handler, and furnace to a reference number and SEER2/EER2/HSPF2.
body_markdown:
HVAC distributors handle equipment matchups online by storing each AHRI-certified combination of outdoor unit, indoor coil or air handler, and furnace as its own record, keyed to the AHRI Certified Reference Number and carrying the system's rated capacity, SEER2, EER2, and HSPF2. Buyers then[reach](https://www.anglera.com/glossary/reach-registration-evaluation-authorisation-restriction-of-chemicals) those records two ways: by entering an AHRI or model number, or by starting from a condenser or heat pump product page and filtering the certified indoor matches by efficiency, tonnage, and incentive eligibility.


What sits underneath decides whether that works. The certified number belongs to the system, not to any single SKU, so the data model has to be built around combinations.


## What an AHRI certified matched combination is


For split air conditioners and heat pumps,[AHRI certifies the performance of the system and not the individual units](https://www.ahrinet.org/certification/cee-directory/how-and-why-certified) . A certified matched system appears in the AHRI Directory as an indoor and outdoor combination, and each one gets a unique Certified Reference Number. The same AHRI page notes that the certificate generated from the directory may be required when applying for energy efficiency rebates, incentives, and tax credits.


That is why a 3-ton condenser has no single SEER2. Its rating depends on which coil, air handler, or furnace it is paired with. Carrier's homeowner guidance makes the same point from the other side: when reading a certificate,[confirm that the outdoor unit, indoor coil or air handler, and furnace match the proposed installation](https://www.carrier.com/us/en/residential/hvac-resources/ahri/) , and check the reference number, rated capacity, and efficiency ratings.


The ratings themselves changed in 2023. Under the federal standards that took effect January 1, 2023, the metrics moved from SEER, EER, and HSPF to[SEER2, EER2, and HSPF2](https://www.ahrinet.org/2023-energy-efficiency-standards) , tested under the appendix M1 procedure, which raises the external static pressure used in testing by up to five times. AHRI notes the M1 numbers are lower than the old ones even though minimally compliant products under M1 are approximately 7% more efficient, and that requirements for residential central air conditioners vary across three regions: North, Southeast, and Southwest. DOE has since amended appendix M1 again, with[the amended version mandatory for testing starting July 7, 2025](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/consumer-central-air-conditioners-and-heat-pumps) . For a distributor, the practical consequence is simple: a matchup row with an old SEER value and no SEER2 is a stale row, and because minimums vary by region, a combination that meets the standard in one region can fall short in another, so eligibility belongs on the matchup row.


## How HVAC distributor websites present system matchups


Looking at the public sites that currently answer this question, three patterns repeat.


**Search by number.** Ferguson's AHRI lookup lets logged-in contractors[search by model number or AHRI number](https://www.ferguson.com/content/pro-services/online-services/ahri-matchup-tool/) across split heat pump and split AC systems from brands including Goodman, Rheem, and Trane. LennoxPros offers both an[AHRI number search and a systems search](https://www.lennoxpros.com/ahri) , and Carrier points users to the AHRI Directory to search by reference number or model number.


**Start from the outdoor unit.** East Coast Metal Distributors puts its AHRI lookup[on outdoor equipment product pages](https://www.ecmdi.com/using-our-website/ahri-matchups) . The buyer picks a matching air handler, indoor coil, furnace plus coil, or mobile home coil, gets a list of matchups with certificate numbers, filters by efficiency, capacity, energy use, and tax eligibility, then adds the outdoor unit, indoor unit, and accessories to the cart together.


**Guided selector with commerce attached.** Gemaire's[AHRI Matchups Selector](https://www.gemaire.com/matched-systems) starts from equipment type, SEER rating, tonnage, and brand, then shows certified systems with specs, parts lists, inventory, and pricing. The LennoxPros tool filters outdoor units by phase, location, voltage, refrigerant (R-410A, R-454B, R-32), tonnage, and SEER2/EER2/HSPF2, and filters indoor units by furnace efficiency, air handler or coil-only, and coil position (upflow, downflow, horizontal).


Separately, contractor software such as AirMatch lists[Carrier, Lennox, Goodman, Trane, and Rheem among its supported brands and says that brand data is updated automatically](https://www.airmatchpro.com/brands) . So a distributor's matchup data can end up side by side with what the contractor already sees in a proposal tool. If the two disagree, the distributor risks losing the quote.


## The data model behind a matchup tool


Every one of those front ends depends on the same back end: a combination table that references product SKUs, plus clean attributes on each SKU so the filters work. Here is the minimum field map.


Record Fields that have to be right


Matchup (one row per certified combination)` ahri_ref_number` ,` outdoor_model` ,` indoor_model` ,` furnace_model` (nullable),` system_type` (split AC, split HP),` rated_cooling_btuh` ,` seer2` ,` eer2` ,` hspf2` (heat pumps),` regional_eligibility` ,` certificate_status`


Outdoor unit SKU` nominal_tons` ,` refrigerant` ,` voltage` ,` phase` ,` stage_type` ,` brand` ,` series`


Indoor coil / air handler SKU` configuration` (cased, uncased, multi-position),` airflow_orientation` ,` cabinet_width_in` ,` refrigerant` ,` metering_device`


Furnace SKU` afue` ,` input_btuh` ,` blower_type` ,` cabinet_width_in`


Three relationships trip people up.


First, the AHRI reference number lives on the combination, never on a SKU. A distributor that stores "AHRI number" as a single attribute on the condenser has encoded the wrong thing, and the efficiency shown on that product page is meaningless without the paired indoor model.


Second, model numbers in the directory and SKUs in the ERP often do not line up character for character. A directory listing can show a base model while the ERP carries a full model with a voltage or revision suffix, or a vendor part number. The join from` outdoor_model` to your[item master](https://www.anglera.com/glossary/item-master) needs an explicit mapping, not a string match.


Third, refrigerant now has to agree across the system. With R-454B and R-32 equipment arriving alongside R-410A stock, an indoor coil's` refrigerant` and` metering_device` fields decide whether a combination is even installable. Our post on[the A2L transition and product data](https://www.anglera.com/blog/hvac-a2l-transition-product-data) covers which attributes changed.


For illustration, a single brand with 40 outdoor SKUs averaging 60 certified indoor combinations each is 2,400 matchup rows. Multiply by four or five brands and you are maintaining roughly 10,000 to 12,000 rows that change whenever a manufacturer adds a coil, retires a model, or recertifies a line.


## What goes wrong on distributor sites


- **Ratings on the wrong object.** A product page that shows one SEER2 for a condenser, with no indoor model named, invites a contractor to quote an efficiency the installed system will not have. If a rebate depends on the certificate, the homeowner finds out late.
- **Matchups that point at SKUs you do not stock.** The certified coil exists, but your item master carries a different revision, so the selector returns a system that cannot be added to cart, or worse, silently swaps a near match.
- **Filters that return nothing.** If` nominal_tons` is blank on half your air handlers, or orientation is buried in a description string like "MP 3T 21in", the Lennox-style filter on coil position simply cannot run. The matchup table is fine; the SKU attributes are not. Our[HVACR attributes guide](https://www.anglera.com/blog/hvacr-attributes) lists the fields that drive these filters.
- **Stale rows.** Matchup files are a snapshot. LennoxPros dates its data and tells users to check AHRI for the most current matchups, which is the honest posture. Rows that never get re-pulled drift.


## How to decide what to build


If you sell one or two brands and the manufacturer already runs a dealer tool, linking to it and showing the certified number on a system bundle page may be enough. If you sell multiple brands and want contractors to build systems in your cart, you need your own combination table, refreshed from manufacturer matchup files and checked against the AHRI Directory, joined to an item master whose SKUs carry clean tonnage, refrigerant, orientation, width, and voltage.


The second option is mostly attribute work, and it is ongoing. That is the part that is easy to underestimate. Your PIM or ERP can store the combinations, but someone has to extract` cabinet_width_in` from a coil spec sheet, normalize "R454B" and "R-454B", reconcile directory model strings to your SKUs, and flag the rows where the manufacturer's literature and your item master disagree. That is the work Anglera does: it pulls values from the actual spec sheets and manufacturer pages, scores each one for confidence, and routes conflicts to a reviewer instead of guessing, alongside whatever PIM, ERP, or flat file you already run. See[how Anglera works](https://www.anglera.com/how-it-works) for the mechanics.


In practice, a matchup tool is only as good as the SKU attributes it filters on and the mapping between directory models and your item master.
